title: Homiliae In Lucam
author: Origen
source: Translated by Claude from tlg2042.tlg016.opp-grc1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: < Ὡς πρὸς τὸ ῥητόν, ὁπλισώμεθα κατὰ τῶν ἀθέων αἱρέσεων λεγουσῶν, ὅτι οὐχ ὁ Δημιουργὸς πατὴρ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ οὐδὲ ὁ θεὸς τοῦ νόμου, οὐδὲ ὁ θεὸς τοῦ ναοῦ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ πατὴρ τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Τῆς γὰρ φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούοντες οἱ ἀπὸ Οὐαλεντίνου αἰδείσθωσν λέγοντος· λέγοντος· τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου δεῖ εἶναί με <, εἰ προσίενται τὸ ῥητόν.
passages.english: As regards the literal sense, let us arm ourselves against the godless heresies which say that the Creator is not the Father of Jesus Christ, and that neither the God of the Law nor the God of the Temple is the Father of Christ. For let the followers of Valentinus, when they hear his voice saying, "I must be in the [house] of my Father," be put to shame, if they accept the literal sense.
passages.notes: The edition's angle brackets mark a fragment set off in the printed text; they are omitted here. "λέγοντος" is printed twice, an evident duplication, and "αἰδείσθωσν" is read as αἰδείσθωσαν. "τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου" (Luke 2:49) literally means "in the things of my Father"; the argument here takes it as "my Father's house", that is, the Temple.

passages.original: Si videris haereticos dogmatum suorum mendacium pro pane comedere, scito lapidem eorum esse sermo- nem, quem monstrat diabolus. Neque vero existimes unum eum habere lapidem; habet plures lapides, de quibus a Matthaeo in- troducitur loquens: >fic, ut lapides isti panes fiant <. Dixit Marcion, et lapis diaboh ei factus est panis. Dixit Valentinus, et ahus lapis ei versus est in panem, Habuit et Basihdes ejusmodi panem et ceteri haeretici. Unde sollicite providendum, ne forte diaboh lapidem comedentes pute- mus nos pane vesci Dei.
passages.english: If you see heretics eating the lie of their doctrines in place of bread, know that their teaching is the stone which the devil shows. And do not suppose that he has only one stone; he has many stones, about which Matthew introduces him as saying: "Command that these stones become loaves." Marcion spoke, and the devil's stone became bread for him. Valentinus spoke, and another stone was turned into bread for him. Basilides too had bread of this kind, and so did the other heretics. Therefore we must take careful precautions, lest by chance, while eating the devil's stone, we think we are feeding on the bread of God.
passages.notes: Although labelled Greek, this passage is Latin; it is presumably Jerome's Latin version of Origen. Scanning errors have been corrected silently: "fic" is read as "dic", "diaboh" as "diaboli", "ahus" as "alius" and "Basihdes" as "Basilides". With "dic", the quotation literally means "Say that these stones become loaves" (Matt. 4:3, plural form).
